order: Ranks 1, 2, 4 and 5 are one beach in Balatonfüred, and tier 2 ranks 10, 11, 12 and 22 are the same beach again. Eight of the twenty-three rows in the country describe a single 500 m strip.

Rank 1 is a hotel's private beach; rank 8 is a food counter inside a water park; rank 6 is a campsite business; rank 7 is an inland village pool. Four of the nine tier-1 rows are not public beaches at all.
Siófok, the biggest resort on the lake, has no row at any tier, so Hungary's beach list opens without the place most Hungarians would name first.

Keszthelyi Városi Strand (tier 2 rank 19) and the Tihany Napsugár beach (tier 2 rank 23) are both genuinely notable and sit below a Győr oxbow, a Danube picnic island and two Szeged riverside duplicates.
Lake Velence and Lake Tisza, the country's second and third bathing lakes, are absent while the Tisza riverbank at Szeged holds three rows.

order: Rank 1 is a public park inside Budapest. Ranks 8 to 12 are five small hills in the Visegrád and Esztergom cluster.
The Mátra, which contains both of Hungary's highest summits, contributes nothing to either tier. The Bükk and the Börzsöny contribute nothing either.
Three of the twelve tier-1 rows (Jakab-hegy, Tubes, Misina) are the same Mecsek ridge above Pécs, which is defensible individually but takes a quarter of the country's top list for one city.
Tokaji-hegy at rank 4 and Nagy-Eged hegy at rank 5 are good, well-chosen entries: both are real landmark hills of famous wine regions.
Szent György-hegy, a genuine Balaton-uplands landmark, sits at tier 2 rank 19 under a broken half-translated name, below several forest knolls.

counts_verdict: Both counts are too low and, more importantly, mostly duplicates. 23 beaches for a country whose entire summer culture is Lake Balaton is far too few, and after dedupe it is roughly eight distinct places, because eight rows are one Balatonfüred strip and four more are Szeged and Győr riverside pairs. Siófok, Balatonalmádi, Fonyód, Szigliget, Révfülöp, Zamárdi's real beach, Lake Velence and Lake Tisza are all absent. Nine tier-1 beach slots for Hungary is about right in size; the problem is that four of them are not beaches. 58 mountains is a fair volume for a country this flat, but the distribution is wrong: ten rows come from the Visegrád hills and none from the Mátra, the Bükk or the Börzsöny, and the tier-1 count of 12 includes a city park and four forest knolls.
top_pick_verdict: No on both. top_beach is 'Annabella Strand', a hotel's private beach in Balatonfüred, which is both a hospitality row and one of eight duplicates of the same strip; the country card should carry Siófok Nagystrand for the resort image or Tihany for the scenic one. top_mountain is 'Gellért Hill', a 235 m park in Budapest; it should be Kékes as the highest point, or Badacsony or Dobogó-kő if the card wants a picture worth looking at. Both current picks are absent-canon failures: the right answer in each case is not merely ranked low, it is not in the file at all.
notes: Hungary shows the duplicate failure mode more severely than Bulgaria's Nesebar case: one Balatonfüred beach is present eight times, under Hungarian, part-English and trading-name variants, and it takes four of the nine tier-1 slots plus the country's top_beach. A name-normalising, geo-clustered dedupe at roughly 150 m would collapse it. The hospitality problem is also systematic here rather than incidental: the venue names that leak in are exactly the ones with a business suffix (Kemping és Apartman, Gastro, Mike's, Strandoase) or an OSM leisure=water_park tag, both of which are cheap to filter. On the mountain side the ranking clearly rewards OSM node density, which is why the Visegrád hills, well mapped and close to Budapest, dominate while the Mátra, the Bükk and the Börzsöny are missing entirely. There is also a name-mangling bug to catch separately: 'Szent György-hill' has had its Hungarian suffix machine-translated, which is the same class of defect as Poland's 'Kasprov vrch / Kasprowy Wierch' string.
